title: Left Atrial Functional Parameters and Left Ventricular Reverse Remodeling After Aortic Valve Replacement in Severe Aortic Stenosis.
authors: Na Chen; Yongxin Li; Siqi Cao; Wenhui Gu; Huiyu Tang; Siyao Sun; Tao Cong; Haibo Wu; Jun Wu
abstract:
Left ventricular reverse remodeling (LVRR) after aortic valve replacement (AVR) varies in severe aortic stenosis (AS). We evaluated whether preoperative left atrial (LA)-derived functional indices were associated with structural LVRR (S-LVRR) and functional LVRR (F-LVRR).
This retrospective 2-center study included 139 adults with severe AS undergoing surgical or transcatheter AVR and follow-up echocardiography after a median of 6.1 months. S-LVRR was defined as normalization of left ventricular (LV) mass index, and F-LVRR as sex-specific recovery of absolute LV global longitudinal strain. Separate adjusted logistic models assessed LA reservoir strain (LASr), LA stiffness index (LASI), LA reservoir work, and LA volumetric/mechanical coupling index, with supportive sensitivity analyses.
S-LVRR and F-LVRR occurred in 58 (41.7%) and 42 (30.2%) patients, respectively. Higher LASr and lower LASI were independently associated with S-LVRR (odds ratio [OR] per 1-standard deviation increase, 2.48; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.37-4.49 and OR, 0.32; 95% CI, 0.13-0.79) and F-LVRR (OR, 7.41; 95% CI, 2.70-20.32 and OR, 0.01; 95% CI, 0.00-0.15). LASr remained robust across sensitivity analyses, whereas LASI was attenuated in change-based analyses.
In severe AS, preserved preoperative LASr and lower LASI were associated with postoperative LVRR after AVR. LASr was the most consistent LA-derived marker and may complement conventional LV assessment pending prospective validation.

title: The Art Behind the Algorithm: Hybrid Ablation and the Need for a Lifetime Strategy in Non-Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation.
authors: Cristiano Spadaccio; Stefano Schena; Andrew J Sherman
journal: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology
abstract: The management of persistent and long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation remains highly variable in clinical practice, despite increasingly refined guidelines and an expanding ablation armamentarium. Treatment sequencing is frequently driven by local program infrastructure and institutional culture, and hybrid ablation is often deferred until multiple endocardial procedures have failed, by which point progressive atrial remodeling may have already narrowed the therapeutic window. Randomized and registry data support a meaningful role for hybrid ablation earlier in the disease course of selected patients with non-paroxysmal AF, particularly those with enlarged atria, prolonged AF duration, advanced substrate, or failed prior endocardial ablation. Contemporary pulsed-field ablation technology has improved procedural safety and efficiency, yet freedom from recurrence at one year in persistent AF remains substantially lower than in paroxysmal AF across all current energy platforms, reflecting the complexity of atrial substrate over time. This ongoing myocardial remodeling places non-paroxysmal AF closer to a chronic structural cardiac disease than to a discrete procedural target and demands a lifetime management strategy rather than a sequence of isolated procedural decisions. The mindset for other progressive structural cardiac diseases has already moved in this direction-aortic valve stenosis is now managed through a multidisciplinary team that integrates anatomy, timing, procedural durability, and long-term risk across the full patient trajectory. We propose an AF Heart Team framework for non-paroxysmal AF in which catheter-based, hybrid, and surgical strategies are selected according to disease phenotype and lifetime trajectory, with the goal of intervening before advanced remodeling reduces the likelihood of durable rhythm control.

title: Variations in Access to Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation Versus Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement by Socioeconomic Factors: A Retrospective Population-Level Study in New South Wales, Australia.
authors: Md Shajedur Rahman Shawon; Jonathon B Ryan; Louisa Jorm
abstract:
Despite increasing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) activity in Australia in recent years, patient access to TAVI remains limited and is often more complex than access to surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). The aim of this study was to identify socioeconomic factors associated with the likelihood of receiving TAVI versus SAVR in New South Wales (NSW), Australia.
Data from the NSW Admitted Patient Data Collection were used to compare the clinical and socioeconomic profiles of patients aged ≥65 years who underwent either TAVI or SAVR between 1 November 2017 and 28 February 2022. Multiple logistic regression analyses were performed on the overall patient cohort and on subgroups defined by age groups, hospital type and funding type.
The study included 6,493 patients (mean age: 79.1 years, 35.5% female) who underwent aortic valve replacement (SAVR=3,294; TAVI=3,199). The odds of receiving TAVI versus SAVR increased significantly with age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] for patients aged 85 years and older versus those aged 75-84 years: 12.3, 95% CI: 9.99-15.2). Patients from the most disadvantaged socioeconomic areas had lower odds of receiving TAVI than those from the least disadvantaged areas (aOR:0.58, 95% CI: 0.47-0.73). Patients with private health insurance/Department of Veterans Affairs (PHI/DVA) funding were more likely to receive TAVI than SAVR (aOR: 3.29, 95% CI: 2.61-4.14), with this finding consistent across age groups and even more pronounced in patients treated in public hospitals (aOR: 5.82, 95% CI: 4.40-7.70).
Our study highlights significant variations in TAVI access based on age, socioeconomic status of area of residence, and funding type. These findings underscore the need for policy settings that promote equitable access and ensure that procedural choices for aortic valve replacement reflect clinical needs.

title: [Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting for Coronary Arteritis Induced by Myeloproliferative Neoplasms:Report of a Case].
authors: Zaiqiang Yu; Shuto Watanabe; Kenyu Murata; Yuki Imamura; Masahito Minakawa
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: In a 60-year-old man with a history of stroke, coronary angiography revealed triple vessel disease, comprising left anterior descending artery (LAD) #6-7 with 99% diffuse stenosis within the stent, #11 and #12 with 90% stenosis, and right coronary artery (RCA) #1 stent with 50% stenosis. Cardiac ultrasonography showed 34% left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) without mitral regurgitation (MR) or tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Following median sternotomy, the bilateral internal thoracic artery (BITA) was harvested by skeletonization;however, dissection was confirmed at the distal end of the right internal thoracic artery (RITA). Owing to severe apical adhesions, we decided to perform on-pump beating coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) for this patient. Cardiopulmonary bypass was initiated via proximal aortic arch inflow and bicaval drainage without left ventricule (LV) venting. Subsequently, a left internal thoracic surgery (LITA)-free RITA composite Y-graft was prepared. On-pump beating CABG was performed in the graft design of the LITA-LAD (onlay patch, 4.5 cm), LITA-free RITA composite Y-graft to the obtuse marginal (OM) artery, and AO-saphenous vein graft (SVG)-4 posterior descending artery (PD)-4AV by sequential anastomosis. Many inflammatory cells invaded the RITA and coronary artery, and distal vessel thickening was confirmed but not in the ascending aorta. Coronary arteritis induced by myeloproliferative neoplasms was diagnosed based on pathology. Coronary computed tomography (CT) revealed the patency of all grafts.

title: [Non-anatomic Bypass for Severe Brachiocephalic Artery Stenosis due to Dissecting Aneurysm After Total Arch Aortic Replacement for Stanford Type A Acute Aortic Dissection:Report of a Case].
authors: Hana Fukuta; Ryohei Ushioda; Masahiko Narita; Yuki Setogawa; Hiroyuki Miyamoto; Ryo Okubo; Shogo Takahashi; Daisuke Takeyoshi; Shingo Kunioka; Masahiro Tsutsui; Hiroyuki Kamiya
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: Dissecting brachiocephalic artery aneurysm after total arch aortic replacement poses a risk of postoperative cerebral infarction, yet no consensus exists regarding optimal management. Treatment decisions rely on the patient's condition, degree of true lumen stenosis, and lesion characteristics. We report a case of a dissecting brachiocephalic aneurysm with severe true lumen stenosis following surgery for Stanford type A acute aortic dissection. A 70-year-old man was transferred to our hospital with acute aortic dissection and multiple right-hemispheric cerebral infarctions and underwent emergency total arch replacement. On postoperative day nine, contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed progressive false lumen expansion with significant true lumen compression. To prevent further cerebral ischemia, a left axillary-right common carotid artery non-anatomic bypass was performed. The patient gradually recovered left upper limb function and was transferred for rehabilitation on postoperative day 27.

title: Pearls & Oy-sters: Trace Visualization of the Central Retinal Artery: A Favorable Sign for Late-Window Endovascular Therapy in Central Retinal Artery Occlusion.
authors: Yang Du; Zhongqi Qi; Lu Cong; Dong Wang; Wanhu Liu; Shuo Zhang
abstract: In acute central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), vessel stenosis and hemodynamic impairment significantly affect visual prognosis. We report a 69-year-old man who presented with 18 hours of acute, severe right eye blurred vision. Fundus examination and optical coherence tomography confirmed central retinal artery (CRA) occlusion with inner retinal edema. Digital subtraction angiography revealed an aortic arch variation and severe C1 segment stenosis of the right internal carotid artery (ICA), accompanied by delayed ophthalmic artery filling and faint visualization of the CRA. After multidisciplinary consultation, the patient underwent ICA stenting. Postoperative imaging showed resolved stenosis and improved retinal perfusion; the patient's vision subsequently improved and stabilized. This case suggests that revascularization can facilitate visual recovery even beyond the traditional window. Furthermore, faint CRA visualization on digital subtraction angiography indicates residual flow, providing a potential rationale for recanalization therapy.

title: Lipoprotein(a) in calcific aortic stenosis: mechanistic insights, clinical evidence, and emerging therapies.
authors: Wang Li; Shao Yun Shuang; You Bei An; Xu Yao; Wang Hao; Xu Xing Sheng; Pang Xue Lian; Meng Qing Feng
abstract: Calcific aortic stenosis (CAVS) is the most prevalent valvular heart disease affecting older adults, yet no validated pharmacological intervention can halt its progressive deterioration. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] denotes a genetically regulated low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-like particle, in which apolipoprotein(a) forms a covalent bond with apolipoprotein B-100. Cumulative genetic, epidemiological, imaging and mechanistic research supports a causal role for elevated circulating Lp(a) in the initiation, and suggests a contribution to the advancement, of calcific aortic valve lesions. Lp(a) mediates valve injury mainly via preferentially transporting oxidized phospholipids (OxPL), anchoring within aortic valve leaflets, triggering endothelial activation and inflammatory cascades, as well as stimulating the autotaxin-lysophosphatidic acid (ATX-LPA) axis; collectively these signals drive osteogenic differentiation and mineralization of valve interstitial cells (VICs). Higher Lp(a) levels correlate with incident aortic valve calcification, accelerated hemodynamic deterioration, augmented calcium deposition quantified by computed tomography (CT), and elevated risks of aortic valve replacement (AVR) or all-cause cardiac death. Conventional lipid-lowering agents fail to reverse disease trajectory in patients with established CAVS. Though proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors only modestly cut Lp(a) concentrations, exploratory analyses have delivered preliminary suggestive signals for cardiovascular protection. RNA-targeted therapeutics and oral agents blocking Lp(a) assembly can reduce circulating Lp(a) by 70% up to over 95%, as demonstrated in early- and mid-phase clinical trials. Most notably, the ongoing Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS randomized trial is directly testing whether pelacarsen can decelerate CAVS progression, and no completed trial has yet demonstrated that Lp(a) lowering modifies CAVS disease. This narrative review summarizes Lp(a) biological characteristics, causal evidence linking Lp(a) to CAVS, together with opportunities and unresolved uncertainties surrounding Lp(a)-targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Cardioplegia Strategies in Aortic Stenosis: A Focused Review of Current Evidence for Surgical Considerations.
authors: Minji Ho; Benjamin Chapman; Gianluca Lucchese; Paolo Bosco
abstract: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) exposes the hypertrophied myocardium to cardioplegic arrest in the setting of increased left ventricle (LV) mass, interstitial fibrosis, impaired relaxation, coronary microvascular dysfunction, and reduced perfusion reserve. These abnormalities may increase susceptibility to ischemic injury and complicate homogeneous cardioplegic delivery. This focused narrative review synthesizes physiological and clinical evidence on cardioplegia composition, temperature, delivery route, dosing, redosing, and myocardial protection during prolonged aortic cross-clamping in adults undergoing surgical aortic valve replacement. AS-specific comparative studies remain limited, generally small, and frequently reliant on biochemical markers; meanwhile, larger observational cohorts and contemporary randomized aortic valve replacement (AVR) trials also vary substantially in patient selection and myocardial protection protocols. Although some studies have associated cold blood cardioplegia with lower biomarker release than cold crystalloid cardioplegia, and cold maintenance strategies with less biochemical injury than warm cardioplegia, no formulation, temperature, or delivery route has demonstrated consistent superiority in clinically important outcomes. Limited historical evidence also suggests that body weight-based dosing may inadequately reflect myocardial requirements in marked LV hypertrophy, but no validated LV mass-based regimen currently exists. Therefore, cardioplegia in severe AS should be considered within a comprehensive myocardial protection protocol incorporating composition, temperature, dose, delivery route, redosing strategy, myocardial phenotype, associated valve or coronary disease, and anticipated cross-clamp duration. Prospective AS-specific studies using standardized protocols, LV mass stratification, and clinically meaningful outcomes are required.

title: Risk of Short-Term Stroke in Non-High-Risk Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Haochen Liu; Zhidan Xiao; Jiahao Zou; Xiaoping Peng
abstract:
To compare the incidence of stroke at 1 and 2 years following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) versus surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), aiming to inform clinical decision-making regarding the safety and effectiveness of these interventions.
A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted including 9 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 9865 patients. The primary endpoint was the incidence of stroke at 1 and 2 years post-procedure.
At 1 year, TAVR was associated with a lower incidence of stroke compared with SAVR (odds ratio (OR), 0.77; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.61-0.98; p = 0.03). No significant difference was observed at 2 years (OR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.65-1.17; p = 0.37).
TAVR significantly reduces the risk of stroke within 1 year post-procedure compared with SAVR; however, this effect was not maintained at 2 years. These findings highlight the early benefit of TAVR, while the long-term advantage requires further investigation.
This study has been registered with PROSPERO, registration number: CRD42025636191, https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42025636191.

title: Experimental study of TPU and SEBS additively manufactured leaflets for novel aortic valve polymer TAVI prosthesis.
authors: Alex G Kuchumov; Denis Khoroshev; Aleksandra Kutuzova; Aleksei Baranov; Oleg Krestyaninov; Ekaterina Barbashina; Pavel Zelenchuk; Edward Matjeka; Thanyani Pandelani; Fulufhelo Nemavhola
abstract:
Transcatheter valve implantation is a cutting-edge technology for high and low risk patients with aortic stenosis. Bioprosthetic valves are limited due to several disadvantages as a long-term durability and structural valve degeneration. Polymeric aortic valve leaflet devices represent state-of-the-art technology to overcome limitations of bioprostheses. Nevertheless, more recent biocompatible and biostable polymers have revealed a significant potential. Additionally, 3D additive manufacturing opens new paths for patient-specific design of biomedical implants. Flexible polymers may not only mimic native aortic valve, but also may improve long-term durability. Polyurethanes and styrene polymers are promising materials for modern polymer valves. Nevertheless, mechanical properties of additive manufactured TPU or SEBS leaflets are not properly studied.
Experimental study of TPU and SEBS samples and aortic valve leaflets for novel aortic valve polymer TAVI prosthesis is presented. Tensile tests and compression tests of three types of FDM-printed samples with various filament alignments (axial alignment, transversal alignment, diagonal alignment) were performed. The results of tests confirmed that longitudinal axial alignment achieve a maximum stress compared to transversal and diagonal directions. Compressive tests of TPU and SEBS 3D-manufactured aortic valve leaflets with digital image correlation technology were performed. Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio were evaluated. Moreover, parameters of constitutive models were found.
The TPU tensile specimen exhibits the highest stress/strain values at a speed of 100 mm/min, regardless of the filament alignment pattern. Slightly lower results are observed at a speed of 50 mm/min, which is likely associated with a wide range of plastic deformation. In the case of SEBS, a different pattern is observed: at 500 mm/min, it demonstrates high resistance to fracture, unlike TPU. A comparison of TPU and SEBS specimens at the same speeds and with the same alignment, based on maximum stress values, shows a minimal difference of 4% with the axial alignment at a speed of 50 mm/min; however, when comparing strains, the difference increases to 90%. The results of the compression experiment on aortic valve specimens made of TPU and SEBS at a speed of 30 mm/min showed that TPU force values for is considerably lower (4% of the maximum case), while for SEBS the spread increases to 20% of the maximum case.
SEBS aortic valve leaflets were shown to be stiffer than TPU. It can be a step for choice of stiffer/softer leaflets for patient-specific device. The proposed approach can help manufacturers in elaboration and manufacturing of new TAVI polymer devices design made of TPU and SEBS polymers for clinical applications.

title: Association of CT-Based Sarcopenia, Clinical Frailty, and Nutritional Status With Mortality After Aortic Valve Replacement for Severe Aortic Stenosis.
authors: Jin Ha Park; Hyun-Soo Zhang; Suji Lee; Sarah Soh; Young Joo Suh
abstract:
This study investigated the association between multiple frailty-related markers-Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score, and computed tomography (CT)-based sarcopenia-and overall survival after aortic valve replacement (AVR) for severe aortic stenosis (AS), with particular emphasis on the first year after AVR.
A total of 407 patients with severe AS who underwent surgical or transcatheter AVR at a tertiary center between November 2020 and December 2022 were retrospectively included. Three frailty-related markers were analyzed: CFS score for functional frailty, CONUT score for nutritional status, and CT-defined sarcopenia for structural muscle depletion. The CONUT score was calculated using serum markers, and sarcopenia was defined according to cohort-specific tertiles of the paravertebral muscle index quantified at the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12) vertebral level using CT. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis was performed to assess the prognostic associations of the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) score and the three frailty-related markers with all-cause mortality after AVR.
Within 1 year after AVR, 32 patients (7.9%) died. In the overall multivariable analysis, higher CFS scores and CT-defined sarcopenia were independently associated with mortality, with hazard ratios (HRs) of 1.82 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.40-2.38; P < 0.001) and 2.63 (95% CI, 1.22-5.67; P = 0.014), respectively. The STS score and CONUT scores were not associated with survival, with HRs of 1.00 (95% CI, 0.95-1.06; P = 0.883) and 1.05 (95% CI, 0.90-1.22; P = 0.563), respectively. A significant interaction was observed between the CONUT score and sarcopenia.
Among patients with severe AS undergoing AVR, higher CFS scores and CT-based sarcopenia were independently associated with survival after adjustment for the STS score. The prognostic association of the CONUT score differed according to sarcopenia status. These findings support the incorporation of functional and structural vulnerabilities into risk assessment for patients undergoing AVR for AS; however, the role of nutritional status requires further investigation.

title: New ESC/EACTS guidelines for the management of aortic valve disease: key takeaways and implications of long-term TAVR results based on recent explant and redo-TAVR registry outcomes.
authors: Saptarshi Paul
abstract:
The 2025 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) guidelines for valvular heart disease represent a pivotal update, emphasizing earlier intervention for aortic stenosis (AS) and broader indications for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). These changes are driven by randomized trial data demonstrating TAVR's safety in lower-risk patients. However, as TAVR expands to younger cohorts, long-term durability remains a concern.
This narrative review examines key guideline updates for aortic valve disease, focusing on aortic stenosis (AS) and aortic regurgitation (AR), and integrates insights from recent registries (2020-2025) on TAVR explantation and redo-TAVR outcomes. Data from the EXPLANT-TAVR, EXPLANTORREDO-TAVR and FRANCE 2/FRANCE TAVI registries reveal reintervention rates of 0.3-1.7% at 8 years, with redo-TAVR offering superior short-term survival (30-day mortality 1.5-6.2%) compared to explantation (11.9-13.6%). Structural valve deterioration (SVD), leaflet thrombosis, and endocarditis predominate failure causes, underscoring the need for lifetime management strategies.
Implications include refined patient selection, enhanced imaging surveillance, and Heart Team-driven decisions to balance procedural benefits against reintervention risks.

title: Early recognition of PRKAG2 syndrome in an adolescent with a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy phenotype and ventricular pre-excitation: a case report.
authors: Zonghui Hou; Xuechen Liu; Mengqi Zhao; Junxiang Pan; Feiyang Wang; Chunbo Wang; Lianyi Wang
abstract:
PRKAG2 syndrome is a rare glycogen-storage cardiomyopathy that can mimic sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). The diagnostic clue is not left ventricular hypertrophy alone, but the combination of hypertrophy with ventricular pre-excitation and conduction-system abnormalities. This pattern is clinically important because PRKAG2 syndrome differs from sarcomeric HCM in disease progression, arrhythmic risk, and long-term management.
A 12-year-old boy presented with recurrent exertional chest tightness. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed ventricular pre-excitation, and echocardiography demonstrated asymmetric non-obstructive left ventricular hypertrophy. An external Holter report recorded sinus bradycardia and nocturnal pauses. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous PRKAG2 variant, NM_016203:c.1423A>G (p.Lys475Glu), classified as likely pathogenic. The available report from a clinically indicated invasive electrophysiological procedure documented persistent pre-excitation and localized the earliest antegrade ventricular activation to the right midseptal para-Hisian region. Catheter ablation was deferred because no tachyarrhythmia had been documented and ablation near the His bundle carried a substantial risk of atrioventricular block. During approximately 2 years of follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable, with persistent hypertrophy and no major arrhythmic or conduction events.
In adolescents with otherwise unexplained ventricular hypertrophy, ventricular pre-excitation should prompt consideration of PRKAG2 syndrome and other HCM phenocopies, even without a positive family history. Recognition of this combined structural and electrical phenotype may facilitate earlier genetic diagnosis and guide long-term rhythm surveillance. The mechanism of pre-excitation should be described only to the extent supported by the available electrocardiographic and procedural documentation.

title: State of Art of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation for the Treatment of Aortic Stenosis in Low-Risk Patients: A Perspective on Brazilian Contributions and Implementation Challenges.
authors: Eduardo Keller Saadi; Rodrigo Petersen Saadi; Ana Paula Tagliari
abstract: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has profoundly changed the management of severe aortic stenosis (AS), evolving from a treatment reserved for inoperable and high-risk patients to an established therapeutic option across a wide surgical risk spectrum. Although the expansion of TAVI indications has been largely supported by randomized clinical trials conducted in high-income countries, real-world experience and technological contributions from distinct healthcare systems are increasingly relevant. Brazil has played a significant role in the early adoption, structured implementation, and clinical evaluation of TAVI in Latin America. Since the first procedures performed in 2008, Brazilian centers have developed Heart Team models, contributed to national and regional registries, and generated real-world evidence demonstrating procedural safety and effectiveness comparable to international benchmarks, despite the presence of resource limitations and a higher prevalence of complex clinical and anatomical scenarios. The incorporation of TAVI into the Brazilian public health system in 2022 marked a major milestone in expanding access to minimally invasive therapy for patients with severe AS. In parallel, Brazilian scientific societies have adapted international guideline recommendations to local practice, supporting evidence-based patient selection across different surgical risk categories. Notably, Brazil has also emerged as a developer of locally engineered transcatheter valve technologies, highlighting its transition from a technology consumer to an active contributor in the field of structural heart disease. This review summarizes the historical evolution, national experience, clinical outcomes, guideline integration, technological innovation, and health economic considerations of TAVI in Brazil.

title: Single vs Double ProGlide Devices for Access Site Closure after Transfemoral Aortic Valve Replacement: The SINGLE-CLOSURE Trial.
authors: Xianbao Liu; Yuchao Guo; Guangyuan Song; Tongfeng Chen; Guipeng An; Lihan Wang; Yansong Guo; Hao Zhou; Lei Jiang; Xiaomin Chen; Biao Cheng; Guannan Niu; Kai Xu; Yibing Shao; Zhikui Chen; Yining Yang; Zhenfei Fang; Jinjun Liu; Jiancheng Xiu; Jianying Chen; Yongping Bai; Xiaodong Zhuang; Zhenfeng Cheng; Lei Wang; Jizhe Xu; Xiangwen Liang; Ke Han; Haochang Hu; Qiong Liu; Martin B Leon; Jian'an Wang
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
abstract:
Despite advances in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), access-site vascular complications remain an important source of procedural morbidity. The conventional double-ProGlide strategy may increase the risk of access-site stenosis and other vascular complications, particularly in patients with challenging iliofemoral anatomy. Retrospective studies have suggested that a single-ProGlide strategy may offer an effective alternative, but this strategy has not yet been evaluated in a randomized trial.
This trial aimed to determine whether a single-ProGlide strategy could offer a simpler alternative to the conventional double-ProGlide strategy without increasing vascular complications.
The SINGLE-CLOSURE trial was a prospective, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 25 centers in China. Patients aged ≥65 years scheduled for transfemoral TAVR were assigned 1:1 to single-ProGlide or double-ProGlide closure for the main access site. The primary endpoint was the in-hospital composite of Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC)-3-defined access-site or access-related major and minor vascular complications.
A total of 876 patients were randomized. In the modified intention-to-treat population, the primary endpoint occurred in 57 of 436 patients (13.1%) in the single-ProGlide group and 65 of 430 patients (15.1%) in the double-ProGlide group, meeting the prespecified criterion for noninferiority (risk difference: -2.2%; 95%: -7.0% to 2.6%; P = 0.013; noninferiority margin: 3.19%). Access-related major vascular complications occurred in 2 patients (0.5%) in the single-ProGlide group and 6 patients (1.4%) in the double-ProGlide group. Among the secondary endpoints, individual components of the primary endpoint, access-related bleeding, time to hemostasis, and all-cause mortality were similar between groups. Access-site stenosis was numerically less frequent with the single-ProGlide strategy (5.0% vs 7.9%), whereas additional closure devices might be used more often (2.5% vs 0.9%).
A single-ProGlide strategy was noninferior to conventional double-ProGlide closure for the composite of VARC-3-defined access-site or access-related vascular complications after transfemoral TAVR. Primary endpoint events were predominantly minor vascular complications.

title: Snare-Assisted Traction Technique for Renal Artery Reconstruction in Endovascular Repair of Complex Thoracoabdominal Aortic Aneurysms.
authors: Ren Wei; Hongpeng Zhang; Minhong Zhang; Cunzhe Fan; Jiang Xiong; Xin Jia; Wei Guo
abstract: Renal artery (RA) reconstruction during complex endovascular aortic repair often fails in hostile anatomy because of inadequate guidewire support. We describe snare-assisted traction (SAT), a novel endovascular bailout technique using conventional off-the-shelf devices. By combining distal snare traction with a long femoral sheath, SAT shifts target vessel reconstruction from simple wire guidance to sheath-based structural support. This provides robust stability for wire exchange and stent delivery without requiring specialized, unavailable tools or high-morbidity open conversion. Among 12 patients with severe RA angulation, ostial stenosis, or sac origin, SAT achieved 100% technical success without procedural complications. At median 6-month follow-up, all reconstructed RAs remained patent with stable renal function. SAT offers a safe, reproducible, and universally accessible solution for hostile target vessel access, significantly enhancing the feasibility and clinical safety of complex endovascular repair.

title: Case Report: Refractory childhood-onset takayasu arteritis with digital clubbing and extensive supra-aortic and lower-limb arterial disease.
authors: Fawzy M Abunejma; Leen M Jabari; Marah Nouredeen Hamad; Tamer O Tamimi; Omair Bseiso; Hisham Aziz Dweik; Raed M A Isayed; Hanan Qunibi; Waleed Alzaro; Wasef Alhroub
abstract: Childhood-onset Takayasu arteritis is rare, and its early picture is often too vague to point at a large-vessel vasculitis. We report a 12-year-old girl who presented with 13 days of recurrent severe retrosternal chest pain and diffuse colicky abdominal pain, on a background of six months of exertional fatigue and painful swelling of the right fingertips, without fever, weight loss or night sweats. Examination showed bilateral digital clubbing, a right arm blood pressure below the 5th percentile with left arm and lower limb readings between the 50th and 90th percentiles, an absent right radial pulse, and weak brachial and right posterior tibial pulses. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 110 mm/h and C-reactive protein 82 to 93 mg/L. Computed tomography angiography showed mild concentric mural thickening of the aortic arch with severe stenosis of the right common and internal carotid arteries, near-occlusion of the right subclavian artery, moderate to severe brachiocephalic stenosis, moderate narrowing of the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, and moderate stenosis of the right common and superficial femoral arteries. The abdominal aorta and its visceral branches were spared. She met the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES (Ankara 2008) classification criteria for childhood Takayasu arteritis, and the arterial distribution corresponds to Numano type IIa, together with peripheral lower-limb involvement that the Numano scheme does not cover. Disease progressed on intravenous methylprednisolone, oral prednisolone, methotrexate, aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin, culminating in an 80% stenosis of the right common femoral artery. Adalimumab was started and later replaced by tocilizumab, after which the femoral peri-arterial inflammatory changes resolved on imaging and acute-phase reactants normalized. Blood pressure asymmetry, pulse deficits and the established stenoses persisted. This case suggests that normal inflammatory markers in childhood-onset Takayasu arteritis can coexist with fixed arterial damage, and that judgements about disease activity are better based on clinical findings and serial imaging together than on acute-phase reactants alone.

title: Sex differences in clinical outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a real-world cohort.
authors: Miriam Estévez Táboas; Julio Echarte-Morales; Ernesto José Ruiz Golcher; Carlos Eduardo Sotomayor-Casillas; André González García; David Neuhalfen; Carla Iglesias-Otero; Elena García-Campos Losada; Nazaret Vázquez-Vázquez; David González Fernández; Hugo Prado Prado; Carmen Cuiñas Fariña; Andrés Antelo-Abeijón; Pablo Juan-Salvadores; Rodrigo Estevez-Loureiro; Jose A Baz Alonso; Andres Iñiguez-Romo; Victor Alfonso Jímenez-Díaz
abstract:
Severe aortic stenosis is one of the most prevalent valvular heart diseases in the ageing population, and transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an effective and less invasive therapeutic alternative. Anatomical, pathophysiological, and clinical differences between women and men may influence outcomes following the procedure. This study aimed to evaluate the association between sex and mortality and procedure-related complications after TAVI in a real-world cohort from the Vigo Health Area.
We conducted a retrospective, single-center observational study including 1,065 patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent transfemoral TAVI between 2010 and 2023. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality at 1 year. Secondary endpoints included bleeding, vascular complications, and new permanent pacemaker implantation. Time-to-event analyses were censored at 365 days; multivariable models used complete-case analysis.
Women were older and had greater frailty and higher surgical risk scores than men. In-hospital and 1-year mortality were similar between sexes. Date-based 30-day mortality was 2.4% in men and 3.7% in women (p = 0.225), and female sex was not independently associated with 30-day mortality after adjustment for age and STS score (adjusted OR 1.79, 95% CI 0.80-3.98; p = 0.154). Female sex was not independently associated with 1-year mortality (adjusted HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.69-1.66; p = 0.772). Women had more bleeding in unadjusted analyses, but female sex was not significantly associated with any bleeding after adjustment (adjusted OR 1.61, 95% CI 0.92-2.81; p = 0.093). Male sex remained associated with higher odds of new permanent pacemaker implantation (adjusted OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.03-2.17; p = 0.036).
Sex was not independently associated with short- or 1-year mortality after TAVI. Women had a higher unadjusted incidence of bleeding, whereas men had a higher incidence of new permanent pacemaker implantation that persisted after adjustment. These findings describe sex-related differences in procedural risk profiles but should be interpreted in the context of the observational design and the long study period.

title: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation vs surgical replacement in low-risk aortic stenosis: time-dependent late mortality in a pooled analysis of trials.

title: Impact of preprocedural frailty on long-term mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Yang Zhan; Yue Mao; Xiaolan Tang; Rong Li; Mei Li; Daoxin Hua
abstract:
This study aimed to investigate the association between preprocedural frailty and long-term all-cause mortality in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR).
A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted from database inception to 15 February 2026. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to pool adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Thirteen cohort studies involving 429,827 patients were included in the systematic review. Of these, 8 studies (4,726 patients) reporting comparable adjusted effect estimates were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Preprocedural frailty was associated with a higher risk of long-term all-cause mortality after TAVR (HR = 1.85, 95% CI 1.51-2.25; I² = 39.4%). The association was generally consistent across subgroup analyses stratified by follow-up duration and frailty assessment methodology. Five studies that were not amenable to quantitative pooling because of non-comparable effect formats or data structures showed a concordant direction of effect, with some studies demonstrating a graded relationship between increasing frailty burden and mortality risk.
Preprocedural frailty is significantly associated with increased long-term all-cause mortality in older adults undergoing TAVR. These findings support the incorporation of frailty assessment into routine preprocedural geriatric risk stratification and multidisciplinary decision-making.

title: Late Discordance Between Right Ventricular Fractional Area Change and Free-Wall Longitudinal Strain After Cardiac Surgery Including Tricuspid Annuloplasty.
authors: Takeo Nakai; Yukikatsu Okada; Megumi Takahashi; Kazumasa Adachi; Takashi Muro
abstract:
This single-center retrospective study assessed preoperative-to-late postoperative changes in right ventricular (RV) indices in patients undergoing cardiac surgery including tricuspid annuloplasty, predominantly with concomitant mitral valve surgery.
This retrospective cohort study analyzed 63 patients with paired preoperative and late postoperative echocardiography after tricuspid annuloplasty. RV fractional area change (RVFAC), RV free-wall longitudinal strain (RVFWLS), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), and tissue Doppler tricuspid annular peak systolic velocity (S') were compared over time. RVFAC >35% and absolute RVFWLS >20% were classified as preserved.
Late echocardiography was performed at a median of 47 months. No statistically significant within-patient change in RVFAC was detected (37.9% to 37.4%; Hodges-Lehmann estimate, -1.0 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -3.0 to +0.7; p = 0.231), whereas RVFWLS decreased from 19.2% to 15.7% (median within-patient change, -3.1 percentage points; Hodges-Lehmann estimate, -3.7 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.3 to -2.3; p < 0.001); TAPSE and S' were also lower at late follow-up (both p < 0.001). At follow-up, 30 of 37 patients with preserved RVFAC had reduced RVFWLS.
In patients undergoing tricuspid annuloplasty, predominantly with concomitant mitral valve surgery, preserved RVFAC at late follow-up does not necessarily indicate preserved RV free-wall longitudinal deformation. RVFAC alone may be insufficient to characterize RV function at late postoperative follow-up in this setting.

title: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Grok Responses to Common Patient Questions about Mitral Regurgitation.
authors: Mohammad Al Zein; Joseph El Roumi; Abdelrahman Ahmed; Susan Keen; Gary Parizher; Brian P Griffin; L Leonardo Rodriguez; Bo Xu

title: Beyond edge-to-edge repair for the percutaneous treatment of mitral valve disease.
authors: Filippo Pensotti; Ignacio J Amat Santos
abstract: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is one of the most prevalent valvular heart diseases worldwide. Mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) has become the cornerstone percutaneous treatment for both primary and secondary MR; however, its efficacy remains highly anatomy-dependent, with a substantial proportion of patients deemed unsuitable and others experiencing residual or recurrent MR at follow-up. Looking beyond M-TEER, a growing armamentarium of alternative transcatheter strategies has emerged, including transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) platforms direct and indirect annuloplasty systems, and, more recently, percutaneous chordal replacement/leaflet-based technologies. This review discusses the current evidence supporting TMVR, transcatheter annuloplasty, and emerging leaflet-based strategies, focusing on those technologies most likely to redefine the treatment algorithm for mitral regurgitation over the coming years.

title: [Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting for Right Coronary Artery Spasm During Mitral Valve Repair With Cryoablation:Report of a Case].
authors: Hiroshi Goto; Hisato Takagi
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: A 64-year-old man with medical histories of diabetes, hypertension, and Basedow's disease complained of dyspnea on effort and lower-extremity edema. The patient underwent mitral valve repair and tricuspid annuloplasty for severe regurgitation, cryoablation (Cox-maze IV) and left atrial-appendage closure for atrial fibrillation, and coronary artery bypass grafting to the left anterior-descending branch using the left internal-thoracic artery. Cardiopulmonary bypass was unable to be weaned, and transesophageal echocardiography revealed inferolateral wall-motion impairment. After aortic re-clamping, additional bypass grafting to the posterior descending branch using the great saphenous vein was performed. The wall motion was slightly improved, and cardiopulmonary bypass could be weaned using intraaortic balloon pumping. Coronary angiography was performed immediately after the surgery and detected diffuse right coronary artery spasm. Isosorbide dinitrate was directly injected into the right coronary artery, and the spasm was improved. Bypass grafting for coronary artery spasm might be beneficial to increase coronary blood flow.

title: [Bentall Procedure Combined With Mitral Valve Replacement for Aortic Root Aneurysm and Concomitant Valvular Disease Associated With Persistent Left Superior Vena Cava].
authors: Nozomu Miura; Hiroyuki Suzuki; Takaaki Yamada; Mitsuhito Kuriyama
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: Persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC) is an anomaly of the systemic venous system caused by the failure of regression of the left anterior cardinal vein during embryonic development. The patient was a 76-year-old woman, who presented with dyspnea. Echocardiography revealed aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, and tricuspid regurgitation. Computed tomography (CT) revealed an aortic root aneurysm and PLSVC. During the operation, by directly inserting an additional venous cannula into the PLSVC and snaring the cannula, we were able to secure a satisfactory bloodless surgical field and provide adequate myocardial protection.

title: [Standardization and Education in Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair].
authors: Ichiro Matsumaru; Takashi Miura
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: We performed minimally invasive cardiac surgery for mitral repair (MICS-MP) in 386 of 612 consecutive MICS patients (63.1%) from August 2010 to December 2025 using an exoscope-assisted approach. Hospital mortality was 0.8%.Freedom from reoperation was 96.6% at a median follow-up of 75 months, and 92.3% of patients maintained mild-or-less mitral regurgitation at final echocardiographic follow-up. We present our standardized protocol covering preoperative selection, perfusion thresholds, a 5-step repair algorithm, and a 4-stage step-by-step training program, providing a reproducible framework for safe MICS-MP.

title: [Outcomes of Robotic Mitral Valve Repair in Patients Aged 80 Years and Older with Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation].
authors: Miho Kuroda; Taisuke Nakayama; Yuto Yasumoto; Kasumi Tamagawa; Yuka Higuma; Miku Konaka; Ryo Tsuruta; Yujiro Ito; Yuki Ikegaya; Hiroaki Yusa; Yoshitsugu Nakamura
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: Robotic mitral valve repair (RMVr) may offer a durable and less invasive treatment option for elderly patients with degenerative mitral regurgitation in the era of expanding transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER). We retrospectively reviewed 42 consecutive octogenarians who underwent RMVr for degenerative mitral regurgitation between June 2018 and May 2025. Mean age was 83.0±2.5 years, and 38.1% had preoperative atrial fibrillation. Hospital mortality was 2.4%, and symptomatic stroke occurred in 2.4%. There were no conversions to sternotomy, re-explorations for bleeding, valve reinterventions, or new renal replacement therapy. At discharge, mitral regurgitation was none or trivial in 90.5% of patients, and only one patient had moderate residual regurgitation. Estimated 5-year overall survival was 80.3%, freedom from reoperation was 100%, and freedom from recurrent moderate or greater mitral regurgitation was 89.3%. RMVr was feasible and provided acceptable midterm durability in carefully selected octogenarians. RMVr should remain an important treatment option within multidisciplinary heart team decision-making.

title: [Long-term Outcomes and Treatment Strategies for Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair].
authors: Maria Yamamoto; Arudo Hiraoka; Toshinori Totsugawa; Taichi Sakaguchi
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: We have actively adopted minimally invasive mitral valve plasty (MICS-MVP) since the early phase of its introduction. Between October 2012 and March 2021, we performed MICS-MVP in 264 patients with degenerative mitral regurgitation. The mean age was 58.5 (range, 18~82) years;104 patients (39 %) were female, and 60 patients had concomitant atrial fibrillation. Concomitant procedures were performed in 150 patients, including tricuspid valve surgery in 56 patients, arrhythmia surgery in 59, left atrial appendage procedures in 58, and congenital heart disease surgery in 39. The mean operative time was 254 minutes. Regarding repair techniques, artificial chordae were used in 139 cases;annuloplasty was performed using a full ring in 101 cases and a partial band in 162 cases. The 5-year survival rate was 98.1%, and the 5-year freedom from major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) was 92.8%. There were no cardiac deaths, and 7 readmissions for heart failure. Compared with the fullring group, the partial-band group showed a significantly lower mean mitral valve pressure gradient (p<0.001). By multivariable analysis for MACCE incidence and readmission for heart failure, none of the factors-including surgical technique and choice of annuloplasty device-were detected as significant predictors. In recent years, annuloplasty with partial band and artificial chordae has become our standard procedure to prevent functional mitral stenosis. Further standardization of surgical techniques may contribute to improve long-term outcomes.

title: [Mitral Valve Repair for Traumatic Mitral Regurgitation Following a Traffic Injury].
authors: Hiroya Fujimura; Satoshi Otake; Yuki Toda; Miku Konaka; Eri Kuroda; Kaito Omine; Atsushi Yamashita; Yu Kawahara; Kazuo Abe
journal: Kyobu geka. The Japanese journal of thoracic surgery
abstract: We report a rare case of acute mitral regurgitation following blunt chest trauma. A 48-year-old man with a history of ventricular septal defect repair in childhood had a traffic accident and was hit in the anterior chest. Initial evaluation at a local hospital showed no abnormalities, and echocardiography was not performed. Seven days later, he developed dyspnea and acute heart failure and was referred to our hospital. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe mitral regurgitation caused by chordae rupture and P2-3 prolapse. After conservative treatment for heart failure, mitral valve repair using artificial chordae and annuloplasty was successfully performed, along with a David procedure for concomitant aortic root dilatation. The postoperative course was uneventful, and mitral valve function has remained satisfactory for more than one year. This case highlights the importance of early echocardiographic assessment after blunt chest trauma, even when initial clinical findings are unremarkable, to enable timely diagnosis and preservation of the native mitral valve.

title: Mitral valve disease in rheumatic heart disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, and rheumatoid Arthritis.
authors: Mateusz Lucki; Bogna Grygiel-Górniak; Ewa Lucka; Maciej Lesiak
abstract: Mitral valve disease occurs in rheumatic heart disease (RHD) and selected systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases, but similar lesions may have different underlying mechanisms. This structured narrative review examines epidemiological, mechanistic, imaging, and management evidence, distinguishing established pathways from incompletely validated mechanisms and hypotheses. In RHD, post-streptococcal valvulitis leads to fibrotic remodeling, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening, producing mitral stenosis, regurgitation, or mixed disease. A meta-analysis of 215,552 children and adolescents in endemic settings reported echocardiographically detected RHD in 24 per 1000. In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), typical findings include leaflet thickening, Libman-Sacks vegetations, and regurgitation; embolic complications may occur despite mild valve dysfunction. Among 508 clinically selected patients with SLE undergoing echocardiography, 27.4% had heart valve involvement and 11.2% had mitral involvement. Immunothrombotic mechanisms may contribute to these lesions, but direct validation in human valve tissue remains incomplete. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a prospective cohort found an association with incident mitral regurgitation (adjusted hazard ratio 1.54, 95% confidence interval 1.32-1.81), but not mitral stenosis. Myocardial imaging findings do not establish a causal link to regurgitation. These findings support anatomy- and severity-based assessment in RHD, combined valvular and thromboembolic evaluation in SLE/APS, and assessment of conventional regurgitation mechanisms in RA. The framework informs clinical interpretation within existing guidelines, while proposed disease-specific mechanisms require further validation.

title: Persistent mitral regurgitation due to subvalvular fusion in hypereosinophilic syndrome despite imatinib therapy.
authors: Kensuke Oue; Nobuo Kondo; Moe Kinoshita
abstract:
Cardiac involvement is a major cause of morbidity in hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES). We report a rare case of severe mitral regurgitation (MR) associated with HES in which apparent echocardiographic regression after imatinib therapy masked irreversible structural disease. A 63-year-old man presented with progressive exertional dyspnea and heart failure caused by severe MR. Marked eosinophilia led to the diagnosis of a myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRB rearrangement. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed infiltrative thickening of the posterior mitral leaflet with vegetation-like subvalvular structures. Imatinib therapy rapidly normalized eosinophil counts, and follow-up echocardiography demonstrated disappearance of the vegetation-like structures; however, MR persisted. Because of progressive symptoms, mitral valve replacement was performed. Intraoperative findings revealed firm fusion of the posterior mitral leaflet and subvalvular apparatus to the left ventricular wall. The postoperative course was uneventful. This case highlights that apparent regression of valvular lesions after imatinib therapy does not necessarily indicate reversibility of structural disease in HES.
To understand that hypereosinophilic syndrome can cause irreversible subvalvular fusion leading to persistent mitral regurgitation despite adequate medical therapy, including imatinib. This case highlights the importance of careful echocardiographic evaluation of subvalvular involvement and timely consideration of surgical intervention when structural valvular damage progresses.

title: Tricuspid Regurgitation, the Once-Forgotten Valve: Current Management Options and Remaining Gaps After the 2025 European Society of Cardiology Guidelines Update.
authors: Alessandro Cafaro; Amir Tahoun; Marco Mussardo; Alessandro Mandurino-Mirizzi; Luca Quarta; Francesco Rizzo; Antonio Tondo; Fortunato Iacovelli; Dionigi Fischetti; Giuseppe Colonna
abstract: Historically considered a "neglected" valvular disease, moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is now recognized as an important contributor to morbidity, mortality, and right-sided heart failure (HF). Natural history studies show that significant TR is frequently associated with left-sided valve disease, particularly mitral valve disease, and independently predicts poor outcomes as severity increases. The 2025 European Society of Cardiology (ESC)/European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease place unprecedented emphasis on TR, elevating this condition from a secondary afterthought to a central element of comprehensive valvular therapy. This reflects an evolution of evidence over the past decade, underscored by increased diagnostic sensitivity through multimodal imaging and the development of novel therapeutic options. However, gaps in the existing evidence persist, and addressing these uncertainties will support future research. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the evidence on TR, incorporates updates from the latest European guidelines, focuses on the most relevant and controversial aspects of patient selection, and identifies key areas where knowledge is insufficient. Furthermore, this review revisits the historical foundations of tricuspid valve research, highlighting how several anatomical concepts fundamental to contemporary interventions were already described as early as the 17th century, underscoring the long-standing scientific interest in this once "forgotten" valve.

title: Case Report: Impella CP-protected percutaneous coronary intervention of the last remaining vessel-a LIMA-to-LAD graft-complicated by no-reflow and rescued with a drug-coated balloon.
authors: Fotios Toulgaridis; Stavros Tzortzis; Nikolaos Tsiamis; Konstantinos Sassalos; Nikolaos Karanikolas; Ioannis Mavrogenis; Anastasia Kitsiou; Georgios Triantis
abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of the last remaining conduit in a patient with severely impaired left ventricular function is among the most hazardous procedures in contemporary interventional cardiology, as any interruption of flow essentially constitutes a global ischemic insult. We describe a 77-year-old man, a former heavy smoker with an 80-pack-year smoking history, who had undergone three-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) 22 years previously. His medical history also included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, severe heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25-30%, and severe mitral regurgitation (MR). At presentation, he had Canadian Cardiovascular Society class III angina and New York Heart Association class III symptoms. The most recent coronary angiogram, performed 6 months earlier, demonstrated chronic total occlusion (CTO) of both saphenous vein grafts, in addition to CTO of all three native epicardial coronary arteries. Thus, the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft to the left anterior descending artery (LAD) represented the sole functional conduit, directly perfusing the LAD territory and supplying the right coronary and circumflex territories through primarily septal and epicardial collaterals, respectively. The LAD displayed two sequential severe stenoses (≥80% each), one at the distal LIMA-LAD anastomosis and another further distally in the native vessel. In accordance with current coronary revascularization guidelines, the Heart Team recommended evaluation by cardiac surgeons. Two independent cardiothoracic surgeons declined redo CABG as a viable therapeutic option. Complex and high-risk indicated PCI (CHIP) was therefore considered the only feasible revascularization strategy. Additional hemodynamic support with percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (pMCS) was deemed necessary. Residual MR and arrhythmic risk, including the potential indication for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), were planned to be reassessed 3 months after successful percutaneous revascularization. CHIP was performed under full hemodynamic support with a continuous-flow microaxial pump (Impella CP with SmartAssist) inserted via the left femoral artery, while coronary intervention was performed through the ipsilateral radial artery using a 6-F IMA guiding catheter. The lesions were successfully crossed with a workhorse wire, despite substantial technical difficulty and with the aid of a microcatheter; however, distal flow was immediately lost, and intracoronary nitroglycerin failed to restore it. Balloon angioplasty restored flow only partially, and a decision was made to proceed with stent implantation. However, stent delivery proved challenging, requiring a guide-extension catheter to be advanced deep into the LIMA body using the so-called 'inchworming technique.' Despite successful implantation of the first drug-eluting stent (DES) at the distal anastomotic lesion, a second DES could not be advanced to the more distal native LAD lesion, despite the use of multiple guidewires and supportive guiding-catheter strategies. Therefore, a drug-coated balloon (DCB) was used as a bailout strategy, immediately restoring TIMI grade 3 flow and leaving only a minor, non-flow-limiting type B dissection. Impella support was discontinued early because of access-related left lower-limb ischemia, and successful percutaneous hemostasis was achieved using a suture-based closure technique. Peak high-sensitivity troponin I, measured the following evening, was 10,800 pg/mL. The patient was discharged ambulatory on day 2 and remained asymptomatic at 3-month follow-up, when an ICD was implanted for primary prevention. This case illustrates the critical role of pMCS in maintaining hemodynamic stability when native coronary flow is lost during PCI of the last remaining conduit and highlights the value of DCB angioplasty as a bailout strategy when stent delivery is not feasible.

title: Efficacy of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors on functional mitral regurgitation associated with heart failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
authors: Charlie Kajo; Ahmed J Alaraibi; Osama T Almutairi; Yaqeen H Alaraibi; Abdullah Alibrahim; Yousef Kh A Almutawah; Salem W S Alasfar; Mustafa Wasif Ali; Aseel Hajjiri; Mohammad Alqaryuti; Abdullatif Alfehaid; Dana Arekat
abstract:
Functional mitral regurgitation (FMR) commonly complicates heart failure (HF) and portends a poor prognosis. While sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) improve clinical outcomes and induce cardiac reverse remodeling in HF, their specific effect on FMR associated with HF severity remains uncertain.
Five databases were searched from inception to 21 July 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating SGLT2i in adult patients with HF and chronic FMR on background guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). Primary outcomes were changes from baseline in effective regurgitant orifice area (EROA) and regurgitant volume (RV). Secondary clinical outcomes included HF hospitalization and cardiovascular (CVS) death. Random-effects models were used. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.
Three RCTs involving 455patients were included. SGLT2i therapy was associated with a statistically significant reduction in EROA (MD -0.086 cm2, 95% CI -0.150 to -0.022) and RV (MD -10.87 mL, 95% CI -17.32 to -4.43), but substantial heterogeneity was observed (I2 = 72.5% and I2 = 63.5%, respectively). On leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, statistical significance for both primary valvular outcomes was lost after omitting the EFFORT trial. The certainty of evidence was rated as low.
Addition of SGLT2i to GDMT was associated with reductions in FMR severity in pooled analyses; however, these findings were not robust in sensitivity analyses and are limited by low certainty of evidence. The apparent reduction in clinical events requires cautious interpretation due to event sparsity. These results should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory, warranting further validation in large-scale, prospective trials.

title: Intraprocedural evaluation of residual mitral and tricuspid regurgitation after transcatheter edge-to-edge repair.
authors: Annalisa Pasquini; Valeria Cammalleri; Andrea Pica; Monica Filice; Annamaria Tavernese; Andrea Stefanini; Daniela Di Lisi; Federica Ilardi; Matteo Lisi; Alessandro Malagoli; Giulia Elena Mandoli; Davide Margonato; Gemma Salerno; Maria Concetta Pastore; Simona Sperlongano; Luigi P Badano; Eustachio Agricola; Antonello D'Andrea; Matteo Cameli; Giovanni Benfari; SIC (Italian Society of Cardiology) Echocardiography Study Group
abstract:
Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) has emerged as an established therapeutic option for selected patients with severe mitral (MR) and tricuspid regurgitation (TR), supported by expanding clinical evidence. However, intraprocedural assessment of residual regurgitation remains challenging because of dynamic hemodynamic changes, device-related artefacts, and limitations of conventional echocardiographic parameters.
This review summarizes current evidence on multiparametric echocardiographic and hemodynamic assessment during mitral (M-TEER) and tricuspid (T-TEER) procedures, with a focus on the evaluation of residual regurgitation, the immediate physiological response, markers of cardiac remodeling and their prognostic implications. Accurate quantification of residual MR and TR requires an integrated multiparametric approach. Residual regurgitation is associated with clinical outcomes and reverse remodeling. Conventional two-dimensional measures are limited by altered post-procedural jet geometry and multiple residual jets. Three-dimensional vena contracta area provides improved visualization and quantification of residual regurgitation, enabling summation of multiple jets. However, its quantitative accuracy has been validated only to a limited extent and thresholds after TEER are not standardized. Volumetric quantification is independent of jet geometry but remains insufficiently validated intraprocedurally. Atrial pressures, venous flow and forward flow describe the physiological response rather than regurgitant severity.
Intraprocedural evaluation of residual MR and TR after TEER requires expert integration of multiple echocardiographic measures of regurgitation with complementary assessment of its physiological consequences and hemodynamic parameters. Advanced 3D imaging plays an increasingly central role in improving procedural assessment and post-interventional risk stratification, but standardized and validated criteria for quantifying residual regurgitation after TEER are still lacking.

title: Transapical mitral valve-in-ring implantation: Results of the real-world European Tendyne valve-in-ring registry.
authors: Julian Maier; Hendrik Ruge; Markus Krane; Sabine Bleiziffer; Kai P Friedrichs; Efstratios I Charitos; Markus Schönburg; Elmar W Kuhn; Cristina Giannini; Marco De Carlo; Rui Campante Teles; Tiago Nolasco; Martin Andreas; Liliane Zillner; Hermann Blessberger; Thomas Lambert; Ilinca Damian; Michael Grund; Andreas F Zierer; Clemens Steinwender; Jörg Kellermair
journal: Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society
abstract:
Mitral regurgitation (MR) is commonly treated with ring-based annuloplasty. In case of recurrent MR, re-do operations are often denied due to high risk. Transcatheter valve-in-ring (V-i-R) procedures offer an alternative. This study assessed the feasibility and outcomes of using the transapical, repositionable Tendyne valve for off-label mitral V-i-R procedures, as an alternative to balloon-expandable valves like SAPIEN, which face limitations such as paravalvular leakage and LVOT obstruction.
The TEND-RING registry is a retrospective, international study with prospective follow-up, including 16 high-risk patients from eight European centers who underwent Tendyne V-i-R procedures between 2017 and 2024. Procedural, 30-day, and long-term outcomes were analyzed.
Patients were elderly (median age 79.5), predominantly male (81%), with significant comorbidities (STS Risk of Mortality 5.6%, 4.4-7.2%) and severe MR (3 + /4 +). Procedural success was 100%, with no LVOT obstruction or device embolization. MR was reduced to mild or none in all patients. 30-day mortality was 6.3%. Over a median 11-month follow-up, five deaths occurred (31.3%), three from cardiovascular causes (18.75%). Surviving patients showed sustained MR reduction and improved symptoms (89% in NYHA I/II). Ring size analysis suggested a minimum of 36 mm for rigid/semi-rigid rings, while flexible bands allowed successful implantation in sizes as small as 30 mm.
Tendyne V-i-R procedures are technically feasible, effective, and safe in selected high-risk patients with recurrent MR. Ring size thresholds identified may guide patient selection and procedural planning in future interventions.

authors: Sudheer Tale; Soibampahel M; Mrudula K; Ritisha B; Subodh K; Girish S
abstract: A 20 – year – old male without any previous comorbidity presented to pulmonary medicine outpatient department with complaints of dull aching chest pain on right side, dry cough and shortness of breath for the pastone year. He was non vegetarian and had no addictions. On general physical examination his vitals were stableand respiratory system examination revealed decreased breath sounds in the right hemithorax. All his routineblood investigations were normal. Chest radiograph revealed homogenous opacity in the right middle andlower zones. Contrast enhanced computed tomography of thorax and abdomen showed a well defined encapsulatedcystic lesion of size 12x10x14cm with internal floating membranes (water lily sign or Camelotte sign) with masseffect on adjacent lung parenchyma causing atelectasis and compression of adjacent vessels (Figure 1). Hydatid serology (IgG) was positive. Patient was treated symptomatically and referred for surgical intervention.

title: RELATION OF HEART WEIGHT WITH AGE AND WEIGHT OF CADAVER
authors: Jolly Agarwal; Virendra Kumar
abstract: Introduction: Height, weight, and age of person has significant impact on the normal size of heart. These parameters need to be considered when cut-off values indicating the need for treatment or even surgery are established. The aim of present work is to study the relation of weight of the heart with age and weight of cadaver. Material and Methods: The study was performed in the Department of Anatomy, Shri Ram Murti Smarak Institute of Medical Sciences, Bareilly on 30 hearts from embalmed cadavers. The hearts were procured from the cadavers available in our department. The heart was thoroughly cleaned and measurements were taken. Results: The mean heart weight was 223.37 ± 57.78 g. Significant relationship between age of the cadaver and weight of the heart (p=0.0004), weight of cadaver and weight of heart (p=0.0001) was observed. Conclusion: The above study provides valuable data of the heart in our geographical location, which may be useful for cardiac surgeons and physicians.

title: Practical Solutions to Common TAVI Complications
authors: Herbert Kroon
abstract: Aortic valve stenosis Calcific aortic valve degeneration mainly affects the elderly population. Approximately 15% of elderly patients have some degree of aortic stenosis (AS)1. Untreated severe AS will lead to heart failure, angina and/or syncope and approximately half of patients will expire within 2 years after symptom onset1, 2. Historically, open heart surgery was the only treatment for severe AS. However, advanced age was a dominant argument to defer surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was contrived as a less invasive alternative to surgery and to fulfill this unmet clinical need. After the first-in-human procedure in 2002, TAVI matured into a guideline recommended treatment of symptomatic severe AS in elderly patients across the entire risk spectrum3-7. Peri-procedural embolization Operator experience, improved planning and implantation strategies and multiple device iterations including smaller profile, repositioning ability and outer sealing fabric converted TAVI into a reproducible and relatively safe procedure8. However, the “Big Five” of complications in the modern TAVI era remain 1) access site complications and bleedings, 2) paravalvular leakage (PVL), 3) acute kidney injury (AKI), 4) conduction disturbances including the need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and 5) stroke9. Up to 5% of patients suffer a neurological event after TAVI, mainly within the first 48 hours8, 10, 11. This finding suggests a direct causative role with the transcatheter valve implantation itself. Transcranial Doppler and brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies revealed debris embolization towards the brain and new brain lesions after TAVI in the vast majority of patients12-15. Most of these embolizations remain clinically silent at first sight but may be linked to neurocognitive decline and frank dementia16. Embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to deflect or capture embolized debris on its way to the brain and may possibly reduce brain lesions and neurological events including stroke and neurocognitive decline. Part I of this thesis adds perspective to the etiopathology of TAVI related stroke and the mechanism of action of the current spectrum of cerebral embolic protection devices. We also present insights into the microscopic analysis of debris that was captured with filters during TAVI procedures. Vascular access and complications 1 TAVI typically requires large bore femoral artery access. By default, larger arteriotomies are at higher risk for access site complications and bleedings. A completely percutaneous approach relies on vascular access closure devices (VCD) to manage the arteriotomy and provide patent hemostasis. TAVI in low to intermediate risk patients is associated with a major vascular complication rate ranging between 2 and 8%4, 11. The conventional closure technique is based on sutures and most access site complications after TAVI procedures are related to closure device failure17. A collagen plug based closure device was introduced as an alternative to sutures. Part II of this thesis addresses vascular complications and provides information on clinical outcomes with collagen plug-based VCD. TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.
